title: Best Pavers for Ontario Winters: What Freeze-Thaw Testing Actually Means
seoTitle: Best Pavers for Ontario Winters: Freeze-Thaw Explained
seoDescription: All major paver brands meet Ontario freeze-thaw standards; a 25-year driveway needs 80mm pavers, under 5% absorption, and a clear-stone base.
tldr: In Simcoe County, Barrie-area winters can produce 80 to over 100 freeze-thaw cycles per season. Permacon, Unilock, and Techo-Bloc all manufacture pavers that meet CSA A231.2 freeze-thaw standards. What separates a 25-year driveway from a 10-year one is water absorption rate (under 5% is the target for Ontario), paver thickness (80mm for vehicle traffic, 60mm for patios and walkways), and a properly drained base system. No paver brand alone prevents heaving or scaling — the base design and joint sand do most of the work.
intro:
Every spring in Barrie and across Simcoe County, we investigate the same complaint: interlocking driveways installed a few years earlier with pitted surfaces, scaled faces, and lifted units. Homeowners are always surprised. They purchased name-brand pavers, paid a reasonable price — what went wrong?

Most of the time the paver itself is fine. The problem is either the base (wrong aggregate, insufficient drainage) or the joint sand (washed out, never properly polymeric-set), or both. But the paver’s own physical properties — particularly its freeze-thaw resistance and water absorption rate — do matter when everything else is equal. Understanding those specifications is how you read a quote critically and ask the right questions before signing anything.

This post explains what Ontario’s freeze-thaw testing standard actually measures, how Permacon, Unilock, and Techo-Bloc compare in practice for Simcoe County conditions, and what thickness and absorption numbers to look for when you’re choosing pavers for a climate that doesn’t forgive shortcuts.

sections.heading: What Does CSA A231.2 Freeze-Thaw Testing Actually Measure?
sections.html:
When a paver supplier or contractor says their product is freeze-thaw rated, they’re referring to CSA A231.2 — the Canadian standard for precast concrete paving units. It requires pavers to survive 50 cycles of freezing to −18°C and thawing back to room temperature without losing more than 1% of their mass. For Barrie and Simcoe County, where a single winter can produce 80 to over 100 natural freeze-thaw cycles, 50 lab cycles is a minimum floor, not a guarantee of lifetime durability.

The more meaningful number is water absorption rate. Denser concrete absorbs less water, which means less moisture is trapped inside the paver when temperatures drop below 0°C. When water inside a paver freezes, it expands roughly 9% in volume. Enough cycles of that expansion within pore spaces will eventually pit and spall the surface from inside. Most quality pavers used in Ontario target a water absorption rate below 5% by weight. Techo-Bloc’s Blu 80mm, Unilock’s Umbriano, and Permacon’s Mega Bergerac all land in this range, with some premium lines pushing below 4%.

The CSA standard also covers compressive strength: a minimum of 55 MPa for residential driveways. By comparison, standard residential poured concrete runs 25–32 MPa. That higher compressive strength in precast concrete pavers is one reason they handle Barrie’s clay-soil movement better than a poured slab — individual units can flex and resettle after a frost event rather than cracking across an entire surface.

The practical takeaway: all three brands we install meet CSA A231.2. But meeting the standard and exceeding it by a comfortable margin are different things. When you’re reviewing a quote, ask for the specific product’s water absorption figure, not just a blanket compliance claim. You can find a deeper dive into paver material properties at our materials library.

sections.heading: Permacon vs. Unilock vs. Techo-Bloc: How They Compare for Simcoe County
sections.html:
We source all three brands through Carr Landscape Depot in Barrie. Each manufacturer has strong entries and weak ones in its lineup — there is no single best brand across every application. We pick based on the project’s load requirements, the homeowner’s aesthetic goals, and budget constraints.

Permacon is generally the most accessible price point in the Barrie market, typically landing at $4–$7 per square foot at supply. Their Mega Bergerac and Bergerac lines are workhorses — reliable freeze-thaw performance, broad colour range, and consistent stock at Carr. Where Permacon falls short is surface texture variety; their tumbled finishes are less varied than Techo-Bloc’s portfolio, which matters when homeowners want a specific architectural look.

Unilock sits in the mid-to-upper range at roughly $6–$10 per square foot supply. Their EnduraColor Plus pigment technology is a genuine differentiator — colours hold better over 15–20 years compared to standard pigment, which is noticeable on south-facing Barrie installations exposed to strong UV. Beacon Hill Flagstone and Brussels Block are popular for patios and entry features. The Umbriano line, with its full-body colour running through the entire paver depth, holds up well against surface scaling.

Techo-Bloc is the premium tier, running $8–$14 or more at supply for their architectural lines. The Blu 80mm is one of the most specified pavers for driveways in Simcoe County because of its low absorption rate and generous thickness. The trade-off is cost and occasionally lead time — some colours run as a 2–3 week special order through Carr. For a standard Barrie backyard patio of 400–600 square feet, the material cost difference between Permacon and Techo-Bloc is often $2,000–$5,000. Whether that gap is worth it depends on the application, expected traffic load, and how long you plan to stay in the home.

For a full side-by-side on these three brands, including which product lines we actually spec and why, read our Unilock vs. Techo-Bloc vs. Permacon comparison.

sections.heading: 60mm or 80mm: How Paver Thickness Affects Winter Durability
sections.html:
Paver thickness is one of the most misunderstood specifications when homeowners compare quotes. The two common residential sizes are 60mm (about 2.4 inches) and 80mm (about 3.1 inches). The right choice depends entirely on the application.

60mm pavers are appropriate for patios, walkways, and light-use surfaces where no vehicle traffic is expected. On a well-built base, they handle foot traffic and Simcoe County winters reliably. We use 60mm for most patio and entry walkway builds. The slightly lower material cost is justified when you don’t need the extra mass.

80mm pavers are the standard for driveways and any surface that will carry vehicle loads. The thicker profile distributes load across a larger contact area, reducing stress concentration at the joint edges — especially important on Barrie’s clay-heavy soils, where subgrade movement after a hard frost is common. We will not specify 60mm pavers for a driveway. The incremental material cost — typically $1–$2 per square foot more — is small compared to the risk of premature failure under vehicle loading.

Some premium lines come in an 80mm engineered specifically for high freeze-thaw environments, with a denser concrete mix than the same brand’s standard offerings. If you’re comparing quotes from multiple contractors, make sure you’re comparing the same thickness and product line, not just the brand name. A Permacon 80mm Mega Bergerac is a meaningfully different product from a Permacon 60mm Bergerac, even though they come from the same manufacturer and look similar in a photo.

Surface finish also matters. Tumbled or heavily antiqued pavers have micro-fractures at the surface that increase water absorption slightly. For driveways in Barrie, we tend to prefer smooth or lightly brushed surfaces over heavily tumbled finishes for this reason. The aesthetic difference is subtle; the freeze-thaw performance difference accumulates over 15–20 winters.

sections.heading: Why the Base System Matters More Than the Paver Brand
sections.html:
We say this on every consultation: a well-specified paver on a poor base lasts 8–12 years. A mid-range paver on a properly engineered base lasts 20–30 years. The base is where most of the performance conversation should happen, and it’s where low bids typically cut corners.

Our standard base uses 3/4” clear stone over geotextile fabric, with HPB (High Performance Bedding) — also called manufactured sand or chip stone — as the final bedding layer before the paver. Clear stone drains freely. Granular A (crushed gravel with fines) compacts well but retains water. In Barrie’s clay-heavy soil, water retained in the base is the problem — it’s what freezes and heaves the surface upward.

Base depth is project-specific. Soil bearing capacity, expected load, drainage conditions, and frost penetration depth all factor into the design. Barrie’s frost line typically extends 1.2 to 1.5 metres deep, but that does not mean you need 1.5 metres of base material. It means the base needs to be designed so water drains away before it can freeze and cause heave. A qualified contractor will assess the soil and drainage conditions on site. Anyone who quotes a single universal base depth without evaluating the specific lot is guessing.

Geotextile fabric is non-negotiable in our builds. It separates the base stone from the clay subgrade below, preventing fines migration over time. Without it, Barrie’s clay slowly infiltrates the stone base, reducing drainage and load distribution — and within 5–7 years, you see settled spots and rocking pavers. For more on what a Simcoe County base needs to survive winter, our winter damage prevention guide for interlocking covers base design in detail.

sections.heading: Salt, Ice Melt, and Surface Scaling: What Causes Paver Pitting
sections.html:
Surface scaling — shallow pitting or flaking of the top 2–3 mm of a paver — is one of the most common complaints we investigate on failed jobs. It is almost never a manufacturing defect. It is almost always a de-icing chemical problem, compounded by a paver surface that hasn’t fully cured.

The worst offender is calcium chloride. It melts ice effectively down to −25°C, but it creates a concentrated brine that penetrates paver pores and wicks moisture deep into the concrete matrix. When that moisture freezes, it spalls the surface from within. Sodium chloride — regular rock salt — does similar damage, particularly in the first two winters after installation when the surface is still curing and most permeable.

The safest option for pavers is sand or fine grit for traction, with magnesium chloride (MgCl) used sparingly if chemical de-icing is needed — it is less aggressive than calcium or sodium chloride. We advise homeowners to avoid any chloride-based de-icer for at least the first full winter after installation, using sand only that season.

Pre-treating pavers with a penetrating sealer before the first winter reduces water absorption and improves resistance to de-icing chemical damage. Water-based penetrating sealers designed for concrete pavers outperform topical film sealers, which can peel in freeze-thaw conditions. For a driveway in Barrie, plan to re-apply every 3–5 years depending on traffic and UV exposure. Our full breakdown of seasonal paver protection is at the winter damage prevention guide.

sections.heading: What to Check in a Paver Quote Before Signing
sections.html:
When you are comparing quotes for a driveway or patio in Barrie or Simcoe County, a few line items tell you a lot about how a contractor thinks about long-term performance.

Product specification: Does the quote name the exact paver line and thickness? “Permacon 80mm Mega Bergerac Charcoal” is a specification. “Permacon pavers” is not. Vague specifications allow a contractor to substitute a 60mm product for 80mm, or a standard mix for a denser premium one, without technically breaching the quote terms.

Geotextile fabric: If it is not on the quote, ask about it. A $0.15 per square foot geotextile layer is inexpensive insurance against long-term base failure. Some contractors omit it to cut material cost.

Base aggregate type: Ask whether the base uses 3/4” clear stone or granular A. On clay-heavy Barrie lots with poor natural drainage, clear stone is typically the better choice because it does not retain moisture.

Edge restraints: Aluminium or steel spike-down edging keeps a paver field from spreading at the perimeter over time. Plastic snap-in edging is less durable under repeated freeze-thaw stress. If the quote doesn’t name the edging material, ask.

Polymeric sand: Ask which product and application method. Properly installed polymeric sand — vibrated in and activated with water — significantly reduces weed growth and joint erosion. A job done with standard dry jointing sand will likely need re-sanding within 2–3 winters.

We’re glad to walk through our specifications on any project across Simcoe County. Visit our interlocking driveway services page or contact us directly to discuss your site conditions in detail.

faqs.question: What pavers are best for Ontario winters?
faqs.answer: Permacon, Unilock, and Techo-Bloc all manufacture pavers that meet CSA A231.2 freeze-thaw standards for Ontario. For driveways, 80mm thickness is the baseline. Techo-Bloc’s Blu 80mm and Unilock’s Umbriano are among the most commonly specified for high-freeze-thaw environments like Simcoe County because of their low water absorption rates — under 4–5% by weight.

faqs.question: What is CSA A231.2 and why does it matter for pavers in Ontario?
faqs.answer: CSA A231.2 is the Canadian Standards Association standard for precast concrete paving units. It requires pavers to survive 50 laboratory freeze-thaw cycles from −18°C to room temperature without losing more than 1% of their mass. Barrie and Simcoe County winters can produce 80–100+ natural freeze-thaw cycles, so compliance with this standard is a minimum requirement, not a performance ceiling.

faqs.question: How thick should interlocking pavers be for a driveway in Barrie?
faqs.answer: 80mm (approximately 3.1 inches) is the standard for any driveway or surface that will carry vehicle traffic. 60mm pavers are appropriate for patios and walkways only. Using 60mm pavers under vehicle load increases the risk of cracking and early settlement, especially in Barrie’s clay-heavy soils where subgrade movement from frost is common.

faqs.question: Can I use salt or ice melt on interlocking pavers?
faqs.answer: Calcium chloride and sodium chloride (rock salt) should be avoided on concrete pavers, especially during the first two winters after installation. These products penetrate paver pores and cause surface scaling from within when the absorbed brine freezes. Sand or fine grit is the safest option for traction. If chemical de-icing is necessary, magnesium chloride is the least damaging of the common de-icers.

faqs.question: Why do some interlocking patios heave in Barrie every spring?
faqs.answer: Spring heaving is almost always a base or drainage issue, not a paver defect. Water retained in a poorly drained base freezes, expands, and pushes units upward. The solution is a base designed with 3/4" clear stone over geotextile fabric so water drains away before it freezes — not a different paver brand.

faqs.question: Does sealing pavers help protect them through Ontario winters?
faqs.answer: A penetrating sealer can reduce water absorption and protect against de-icing chemical damage. For Barrie driveways, apply a quality penetrating concrete paver sealer before the first winter and plan to re-apply every 3–5 years. Avoid topical film sealers — they can peel in freeze-thaw conditions. Penetrating formulas that work into the pore structure are more durable in Ontario’s climate.

faqs.question: Is Techo-Bloc worth the higher cost compared to Permacon in Simcoe County?
faqs.answer: For driveways and high-traffic areas, Techo-Bloc’s premium lines — particularly the Blu 80mm — offer lower water absorption and a denser concrete mix than standard pavers. On a 20–30 year time horizon, the performance margin can justify the premium. For a backyard patio with light foot traffic, Permacon or Unilock’s mid-range products perform well and the cost difference is harder to justify.
